* fix(nym-api): serve a past epoch's partial signatures from its archived key

Credentials outlive the epoch that issued them by up to a week, but the keys
that epoch was signed with were renamed to `epoch-{id}-{filename}.archived` at
the next dealing exchange and never read again. Both partial-signature paths
therefore refused any epoch but the current one, so material a signer had not
already generated could never be produced - permanently unusable ticketbooks
for that epoch. It matters most for a reset, where the master key changes and
nothing else can serve those books.

The keys are now retained per epoch. `KeyPair` keeps an archive alongside the
live slot, populated at the two points that agree by construction: dealing
exchange hands the outgoing key over instead of dropping it, and startup scans
the archive files back in - so a process that stays up through a ceremony and
one that restarts behave the same. `keys_for_epoch` is the single lookup; the
live slot keeps its validity gate, the archive deliberately does not, since the
chain already settled which shares were verified for a concluded epoch.

Two consequences worth noting. `hazmat_into_secrets` now borrows rather than
consumes, because resharing no longer destroys the key it has to keep. And both
partial routes gate on the *requested* epoch's signer set: an api that has since
dropped out of the group still holds the keys, and refusing it on the strength
of the current epoch alone can leave a past epoch short of the threshold its
aggregation needs.

`ensure_dkg_not_in_progress` is deliberately untouched - serving old epochs
mid-ceremony is a separate gap.

Also renames the ecash key-file surface off the legacy "coconut" name
(persist/archive/can_validate, and the `ecash_key_path` field). Mechanical, and
bundled because it renames the very functions this change extends; the config
alias for `coconut_key_path` stays for backwards compatibility.

* fix(credential-proxy): stop a ceremony poisoning the proxy's signer cache

The credential-proxy carried both defects that were fixed in nym-api but never
had its own half done, and it sits on the issuance path, so a DKG re-run takes
it out too.

`epoch_clients` cached whatever the initialiser returned successfully and never
expires. The moment a ceremony starts the epoch id increments, the new epoch has
no verified shares yet, and the query returns an empty set - which was then
remembered for the life of the process, so the proxy kept failing to fan out
long after the ceremony had finished. It now only caches once the ceremony for
that epoch has concluded, answering uncached before then.

The same initialiser also collected the shares into a Result, so a single share
that was never verified - or that carries an announce address the DKG contract
never validated, since it validates none - failed the whole epoch rather than
being skipped. It now goes through `usable_ecash_api_clients`, the same helper
nym-api uses, which drops unusable shares and logs each one.

`ecash_clients` consequently returns an owned Vec rather than a cache guard
(the uncached path has no guard to hand out), which is what nym-api already
does; both wrappers and their call sites follow, dropping two clones that the
guard used to force.

The "has this epoch's ceremony finished" comparison moves onto `Epoch` itself
as `is_epoch_concluded`, since nym-api and the proxy were about to hold two
copies of it, and gets unit tests there - the proxy cannot test its own use of
it, because `ChainClient` is a concrete signing client with no stub.

* fix(nym-api): serve a concluded epoch's data while a later ceremony runs

`ensure_dkg_not_in_progress` was applied to every ecash route regardless of the
epoch being asked about, so for the 11-22 minutes a ceremony takes (two of its
phases cannot short-circuit) nothing was served at all - including for epochs
that concluded long ago and whose data cannot change.

That turns an issuance pause into a spending outage. The aggregated coin-index
and expiration-date signatures are required inputs to `prepare_for_spending`, so
a client holding an unexpired ticketbook from an earlier epoch, whose local cache
does not already have them, cannot spend it until the ceremony ends. Nothing it
needs has anything to do with the ceremony: the signer set, threshold and keys
all belong to the epoch that issued the book.

The three aggregated-data routes and the two partial-signature routes now refuse
only the epoch whose ceremony is actually running. The partials matter as much as
the aggregates, since aggregation fans out to peers' partial endpoints and would
otherwise still fail on them. `post_blind_sign` keeps the blanket gate: issuing
against a previous epoch is a separate question with its own decisions to make.

Gateways were never affected - `credential-verification` builds its master key
from the DKG contract directly rather than from these endpoints.

`epoch_concluded` becomes `ceremony_concluded` (and `Epoch::is_epoch_concluded`
becomes `is_ceremony_concluded`) throughout. The old name read as "this epoch is
over and we have moved on", when what it reports is that the epoch's *ceremony*
has finished - which is true for the whole time the epoch is in use.

The dummy communication channel's knobs move into one shared `SharedCommState`
handle rather than an `Arc` per flag threaded through the channel, the bundle and
the fixture, and it now models a ceremony in flight so the route behaviour can be
tested at all.

* fix(nym-api): serve a settled epoch before its keys reach the archive

The previous commit lifted the ceremony-wide gate off the aggregated and partial
signature routes, but a request for a settled epoch could still be refused one
layer down, for the first phase of every ceremony.

`invalidate_coconut_keypair` fires at public key submission, while the keys it
applies to stay in the live slot until dealing exchange archives them. The lookup
routed an exact-epoch match through that flag, so during the ~10 minutes of the
first phase the previous epoch's auxiliary signatures were refused - and then
served again afterwards, once the same keys had moved to the archive. Only
material the signer had never generated was affected; anything already in its
storage was served throughout.

The flag answers "may we issue credentials right now", which is not the question
a request naming a specific concluded epoch is asking. `keys_for_epoch` is now a
lookup and nothing else, and the two signature paths establish their own right to
use what it returns by checking that the epoch's ceremony is over. That check
lives at the state layer as well as at the route, so neither depends on the other
being correct - the same reason B10 needed fixing at two layers. Issuance keeps
the flag, and `blind_sign` keeps the ceremony-wide gate.

`KeyPair::keys` is dropped: it was the validity-gated accessor these paths used
to share, and leaving it would invite the same conflation back in. Issuance goes
through `signing_key`, lookups through `keys_for_epoch`.

* docs(nym-api): correct the documented failure cases on the ecash data routes

The partial-signature endpoints gate on the signer set of the epoch that was
asked for rather than the current one, so their documented 400 no longer matched
what they do. The three aggregated-data endpoints documented no failure at all,
though they now refuse an epoch whose ceremony is still running.

Blind-sign, the issued-ticketbook and the spending routes are untouched: they
still gate on being a signer in the current epoch, which is what they say.

bugfix: fix various bugs within nym-api making future re-DKG smoother [vol3] (#7088)

* fix(nym-api): keep a deposit spent after its issuance record is pruned

The only thing standing between a deposit and a second ticketbook was the
signer's local `issued_ticketbook` row, and the stale-data cleaner deletes it
two days after the book it describes expires. The deposit outlives it
indefinitely: the ecash contract records no notion of a deposit having been
consumed, deliberately, since deduplication is a per-signer concern. So once
the row was gone a fresh withdrawal transcript for that deposit was
indistinguishable from a first request, and the same payment minted another
usable book.

The cutoff is date arithmetic on a shared config default, so every signer
running defaults drops the same rows within the same cleaner tick - no
signer-set luck required. The second book is invisible to double-spend
detection, since a new transcript means a new wallet secret and therefore
entirely new serial numbers. And nothing distinguished the second issuance from
the first, so the cycle repeated: one deposit, a ticketbook roughly every nine
days, indefinitely.

The record that a deposit has been paid out now lives in `used_deposit` and is
never pruned, so retention of the issuance data itself stays as short as the
merkle challenge routes need. `deposit_usage` replaces the old lookup and is
anchored on that tombstone, distinguishing three states where there were two:
never signed for, signed for with the share still retained, and signed for with
the share since pruned. The first proceeds, the second returns the stored share
as before so idempotent retries keep working, and the third is refused.

The two writes go in one transaction. A crash between them would leave an
issuance row with no tombstone, which is this same bug reopening for that
deposit once the row is pruned. The tombstone insert is a plain INSERT rather
than OR IGNORE: it can only conflict if the issuance insert somehow did not, so
the write path stays fail-closed even if the handler check is ever bypassed.

Deposits whose records were already pruned before this migration cannot be
recovered - each can be spent once more, and that issuance is what finally
records them. The cleaner is untouched, and the epoch the share was issued
under is deliberately not consulted yet; mixed-epoch shares are a separate gap.

* fix(nym-api): stop the issuance cache replaying another epoch's share

The idempotency cache keyed on deposit id alone. A caller that collected some
shares before an epoch flip and the rest after got the old key's share replayed
from cache and the new key's from everyone else, and a share can only be
unblinded against the key that signed it - so `issue_verify` rejected the stale
one, the caller dropped that signer with a warning, and the collection fell
short of the threshold. Retrying changed nothing, because the cache returned the
same bytes forever. The blanket mid-ceremony gate on this route is what opens
the window rather than closing it: the signers refused during the ceremony are
exactly the ones that sign under the new key once it ends.

Note the failure is a silent drop at the caller, not an aggregation error - the
gap description had the mechanism right and the consequence one step off.

`blind-sign` now takes an optional `epoch_id`, the same way the partial
signature routes already do, naming the epoch whose material is being
collected. A share we hold is served when it was signed under that epoch and
refused otherwise, naming the epoch it does belong to so the caller can claim it
by asking again with the epoch pinned. Callers that send nothing get the current
epoch, which is what they were implicitly asking for, and old ones are
unaffected. Deposits we have never signed for ignore the parameter entirely.

Refusing rather than re-signing is deliberate: one deposit yields one book, and
signing again under the newer key would mint a second against a single payment.

For that comparison to mean anything the row has to record which key signed the
share, and it recorded `current_epoch()` - a cache up to five minutes stale,
while a signer keeps issuing under the key it holds until it derives a new one.
The two disagree precisely in the window this fix addresses. `issuance_keys`
hands out the key and its epoch as one guard, so the handler cannot read them
out of step, and the epoch travels with the share into storage.

The parameter stays inert on the signing path. Issuing under a *retired* key is
a separate capability with a retention policy attached, and it is deliberately
not enabled here - nothing in this change resolves keys through the archive.
Adoption by the in-repo callers is left for a follow-up now that the server side
exists.

* fix(coconut-dkg): end the epoch state machine at InProgress

Advancing an epoch that was already in progress re-saved it with a fresh
deadline, the same id and the same keys. Nothing rotated, so the two-week
`in_progress_time_secs` read like a rotation period while being none: without
operator action a key generation lived indefinitely, and the apis spent a
transaction every two weeks to achieve it. Rotation is `TriggerReset` /
`TriggerResharing`, neither of which comes through here, so this is simply where
the state machine ends. `ensure_can_advance_state` says so, and the query says
the same thing, deliberately in lockstep: a signer that is told it can advance
would otherwise pay for a transaction only to be refused.

The reason to do this now is that it makes the epoch's deadline stop moving,
which in turn makes it possible to record something nothing on chain carried
before: when a key generation came into service. The epoch id increments when a
ceremony *starts*, and the deadline is per-state, so the moment a ceremony
finished was simply not derivable. `Epoch::ceremony_concluded_at` records it,
once, on the transition that concludes the ceremony. Retaining a signer's
willingness to serve the epoch it just replaced needs it, and so does any
eventual pruning of retired key material, which was dropped for exactly this
reason.

An epoch in progress now carries no deadline at all. Leaving one behind would
drift into the past and then read as "expired" to both consumers that treat it
as a cache bound, and each of them would fall back to re-querying the chain on
every single call. `None` gives them the same five-minute validity the two-week
value did through `min`, so nothing changes for them.

That is the shape of the compatibility story generally: an api that has not
updated sees identical epoch-cache behaviour, is told `can_advance` is false so
it stops attempting the extension rather than failing it, and ignores the added
field, since `cw_serde` does not deny unknown ones. Reading the stored epoch
back needs `serde(default)`, so the field is `Option` and the epoch mainnet is
currently on reports `None` - unknown rather than wrong.

`in_progress_time_secs` is left in place, since it is serialised inside every
stored epoch, but marked deprecated so that a new reader has to notice. The two
constructors that must still populate it say why. The generator's matching
`--in-progress-time-secs` flag is removed instead: a flag that silently governs
nothing is worse than no flag.

Schema regenerated.

* refactor(nym-api): plumb the inputs the issuance grace window needs

Groundwork for letting a signer keep honouring the epoch it just stopped issuing
under, for long enough that the rest of the fleet has seen the same ceremony
conclude. Nothing behaves differently yet; the resolution that consumes all of
this lands next.

Signers learn of a concluded ceremony from a cached view of the epoch, and that
cache is what makes them briefly disagree about which epoch is issuable. Its
ceiling was a literal five minutes buried in `CachedEpoch::update`, which is an
odd place for the one number every such window has to be sized against, so it
becomes a config field and is propagated in. `CachedEpoch` keeps holding only
cache state and takes the ceiling as an argument; the channel carries it in a
`CommunicationChannelConfig`, which exists to be the home for the tuning the
channel accumulates rather than a loose field among the caches.

The grace period itself is a second field, defaulting to twice the staleness. It
has to exceed it, and deriving one from the other means a change to either
cannot quietly break the relation. Both defaults are unchanged in effect.

`current_ceremony_concluded_at` exposes the timestamp the DKG contract began
recording in 2bad3f1901, since the trait offers narrow accessors over the cached
epoch rather than the epoch itself. It answers `None` both while a ceremony runs
and for an epoch that concluded before the field existed, and says at the
declaration that callers must read that as "no window" rather than "just now" -
getting it the wrong way round would grant a window instead of withholding one.
The dummy channel gains the same accessor plus a helper to place a conclusion a
given interval in the past, so tests can sit inside or outside a window without
a fake clock.

Also covers the claim that 2bad3f1901 needs no data migration, by deserialising
a stored epoch from before the field existed through `cosmwasm_std::from_json`,
the same entry point cw_storage_plus reads through, and asserting the conclusion
time reads as unknown. Deliberately not backfilled: both available values (the
stored deadline, which recovers the last self-extension, and the migration block
time) would claim a conclusion far more recent than the truth, and each errs
towards granting a grace window rather than withholding one.

* feat(nym-api): keep issuing through a ceremony, under a stated epoch

Issuance stopped network-wide for the whole of every DKG ceremony, and a
ceremony can run for hours or stall indefinitely. The epoch a ceremony is
running for genuinely has nothing to sign with, but the one it is replacing
does, and that epoch's credentials are still being spent for days afterwards -
so there was no reason to refuse. `ensure_dkg_not_in_progress` is gone, and with
it the chain query and the error that existed only to serve it. What replaces it
is a resolution of which epoch is actually in service: the most recent whose
ceremony has concluded, which is the current one ordinarily and the one before it
while a ceremony runs.

Requests may now name the epoch they are collecting for, and a fresh deposit is
signed under that epoch's key, gated on that epoch's signer set. Those three -
what was asked for, what signed, and what the audit row records - previously
could all disagree across a transition, and now agree by construction, since the
key is looked up *for* the epoch that was requested. Holding the key is also the
only trustworthy evidence that an epoch's ceremony produced anything, because
the contract reports every past epoch as concluded whether or not it finished;
an epoch we were asked for but hold no key for is refused rather than signed
with whatever is to hand.

Signers learn of a concluded ceremony from a cached view, so for a few minutes
they disagree about which epoch is in service. A signer that has seen the change
keeps honouring the epoch it replaced for a window measured from the conclusion
the contract now records, which every signer reads identically. Without that,
a client collecting across the changeover has some signers sign for it and the
rest refuse for good, leaving it holding shares it can never add to - and this
change makes that routine rather than rare, since issuing during a ceremony is
the point. The window is bounded and closes for good: signing under a retired
key mints books that verify against shares persisting on chain forever, so it is
offered only for the epoch just superseded.

Inside that window a request naming no epoch is refused rather than guessed at,
because it is exactly when signers would guess differently, and a deposit signed
under one epoch at some signers and another at the rest can never be aggregated.
Outside it, naming nothing means the epoch in service, as before.

Every refusal here happens before the deposit is fetched, validated or signed
for, so none of them spend it; two of the tests assert that by following a
refusal with a request that succeeds. Returning an already-issued share is
deliberately looser than issuing: a share is handed back whenever it is the
epoch asked for, including one no longer issued under, since that consumes
nothing and is how a collection stranded across a rotation is recovered.

Drops the test that had this api sign with an epoch-1 key while the chain was at
epoch 2. That state is now refused, and the assertion it made - that the row
records the key that signed rather than the chain's view - is made in the
mid-ceremony test instead, where it is reachable.

* docs(ecash): correct what a ceremony now does to issuance

The protocol docs still describe the blanket refusal that used to make every
issuance and aggregation endpoint fail for a ceremony's duration. Part of that
was already wrong before this branch: the aggregated-data and partial-signature
routes stopped refusing concluded epochs in d634558030, and archived keys became
readable again in 6c1dd74c73, neither of which reached the prose.

What is described now: exactly one epoch is issuable, the most recent whose
ceremony concluded; a request may name the epoch it concerns and a client
collecting several shares for one credential should, since a conclusion partway
through moves the default; a superseded epoch is refused except within the
bounded window after a conclusion, and inside that window a request naming no
epoch is refused rather than guessed at. The blind-sign walkthrough is
renumbered accordingly, and gains the property a caller most needs to know from
it, which is that none of these refusals spend the deposit.

Also drops two paragraphs that documented defects since fixed: the per-epoch
signer caches pinning an empty set mid-ceremony and requiring a restart
afterwards (fff627bd2c, 5fbe96eef3), and `NotASigner` masking the gate's own
error, which no longer exists. The epoch cache is still described, because the
window above is deliberately sized against it, but the note that an audit row's
epoch lags by up to five minutes is replaced: it is taken from the key that
signed now, not from the cached view.

* feat(clients): state the issuance epoch instead of inferring it

Both in-repo callers resolved the epoch from the chain at whatever moment each
piece of work happened to need it, and never told the signer which epoch they
were collecting for. A DKG ceremony concluding partway through a collection
therefore moved the answer underneath them, leaving some shares signed under one
epoch and the rest under another - a set that can never be aggregated, and one
the deposit cannot be spent on twice to replace.

The epoch is now settled once per collection and used for everything that
follows: the signers asked, the threshold required of them, the keys their
shares are verified against, the epoch stated on each request, and the epoch the
finished book is stamped with. `blind_sign` carries it as a query parameter, the
same way the partial-signature routes already accept one; `obtain_aggregate_wallet`
takes it rather than leaving each share's epoch to chance.

For the direct fetcher the epoch is settled before the deposit is made and
recorded next to it, so a collection resumed after a restart continues under the
epoch its existing shares belong to rather than resolving a fresh one. Rows
written before that column existed resolve it again on resume, which is what
they were doing anyway.

The fetcher also stops waiting out ceremonies. Signers now keep issuing under
the epoch a ceremony is replacing, so the only genuine wait is for the first
ceremony ever, before any epoch has concluded and there is nothing to issue
under.

The proxy resolved the epoch twice per request - once for the auxiliary data it
returns and once, separately, for the shares - so a conclusion between the two
reads would hand a client aux data belonging to a different epoch than its
shares. It resolves once now and threads it through.

* test(bandwidth-fetcher): cover the pinned epoch's round trip through storage

The epoch a collection is pinned to is now a required argument everywhere it
travels, so the compiler already guarantees the same value reaches the threshold
query, the signer lookup, each request and the finished book. The one step it
cannot check is the round trip through the database: a nullable column, a cast
each way, and an `Option` to interpret on the way back. Getting any of those
wrong resumes a collection under the wrong epoch and strands the deposit, which
is silent and unrecoverable.

Two tests, then: a recorded epoch comes back as itself, and a row written before
the column existed comes back as unknown rather than as some epoch. Confirmed by
dropping the recorded value on load, which the first one catches.

Adds the in-memory storage this needed, since the crate had no tests at all
before. Note the pool is held to a single connection: every connection to
`:memory:` is its own database, so without that the migrations land somewhere
the queries cannot see.

Deliberately not covered here: that shares gathered under a pinned epoch
actually aggregate. That needs several signer endpoints and real cryptography,
and belongs to a sandbox rehearsal - which is also the only place the races
around a ceremony concluding can be exercised at all.

* fix: let the proxy issue mid-ceremony, and default to the epoch in service

Two places that kept asking about the epoch being built rather than the one
actually in service, both of which undercut the change that let signers keep
issuing through a ceremony.

The credential-proxy refused outright for the whole of a ceremony, before ever
asking a signer, so none of that reached anyone acquiring through it - which is
every VPN client. Its gate now refuses only when nothing has ever concluded and
there is genuinely nothing to issue under, and it resolves the epoch in service
rather than the current one. That distinction is the point: relaxing the gate
alone would have had it name the epoch under ceremony on every request and be
refused by the signers it asked, which is worse than declining up front.

The nym-api's five auxiliary-data routes had the same gap in a subtler form. A
request naming no epoch meant "the current one", while issuance had moved on to
meaning "the one in service". Mid-ceremony those differ, so a client could
obtain a ticketbook and then fail to fetch what it needs to spend it, having
named no epoch in either case and been answered about two different ones. They
now resolve it the same way issuance does.

That asymmetry did not exist before this branch: issuance used to be refused for
the whole ceremony, so there was no way to hold a book whose epoch disagreed
with the aux-data default. It was introduced by fixing the first half and is
fixed here.

Also switches nym-node-status-api to the same resolution, since it drives
issuance through the proxy's state and would otherwise pre-warm caches for an
epoch that has nothing in them.

Note what the proxy's own endpoints now report: asked for the current epoch, or
for material without naming an epoch, they answer about the epoch being issued
under. Reporting an epoch nobody can be issued under is not useful to a caller,
and a caller that pins it is exactly how a ticketbook gets stranded.

The proxy has no test coverage - `ChainClient` is a concrete type with no stub -
so this rests on compile-checking and review, and belongs in the sandbox
rehearsal rather than being considered verified.

* feat(credential-proxy): let a caller name the epoch it needs signer keys for

The partial-verification-keys endpoint served whichever epoch was current and
offered no way to ask for another. A client unblinding shares needs the keys of
the epoch those shares were issued under, so a rotation between issuance and
unblinding leaves it verifying against the wrong keys - and since the epoch a
share was issued under never changes, that failure is permanent rather than
transient. The ticketbook has been paid for by then.

It now takes an optional epoch, mirroring `master-verification-key` beside it,
which has always taken one. Omitting it still means the epoch being issued under,
so nothing changes for existing callers.

This is the half of that defect which lives in this repo. The rest is in the VPN
app and its api: the app has to pass the epoch its shares came from, and stop
treating the resulting mismatch as permanent - it currently abandons immediately
and leaves a pending row that retries identically on every connect for sixty
days. Neither is fixable from here, but they now have something to thread
through.

Note the parameter is `epoch-id`, not `epoch_id`: this endpoint's parameters are
kebab-case while nym-api's are snake_case. Getting it wrong binds nothing and
defaults silently, so the typed client says so where it builds the query.

* clippy

* feat(credential-proxy): only issue mid-ceremony to callers that state the epoch

Letting the proxy issue during a ceremony creates books belonging to the epoch
still in service, which is not the chain's current one. A caller that omits the
epoch when it later fetches verification material is served the current one, so
once the ceremony concludes it can never unblind what it just paid for - and
that failure is permanent, because the epoch its shares were signed under never
changes. Worse, the stuck request then blocks further acquisitions for that
client.

So the mid-ceremony path is offered only to callers that say they can name the
epoch. `TicketbookRequest` gains `epoch_aware`, defaulted, because absent is
exactly what every client predating the field means. A caller without it waits
out the ceremony, which is recoverable and is precisely what it did before
mid-ceremony issuance existed.

Deciding this per request rather than by configuration matters: a global switch
is wrong for some fraction of installs whenever it is set, has to be flipped by
someone tracking rollout, and cannot distinguish the clients that would be
harmed from the ones that would benefit. This needs no coordination and retires
itself once old versions are gone.

The check is deliberately separate from `ensure_credentials_issuable`. That one
asks whether ecash works at all and also guards the read paths, which issue
nothing and therefore cannot strand anyone - folding the two together would have
refused verification material mid-ceremony and undone the point of serving
concluded epochs throughout.

The capability is self-asserted, which is fine: it is a statement about what the
caller will do next, not a security boundary, and a caller that lies only
strands itself.

Also makes the `503` these routes have always documented real. Every error was
being reported as `500` through `new_plain_error` / `new_server_error`, so the
status a client would match on to recognise "retry shortly" did not exist, and
the two conditions that resolve on their own were indistinguishable from a
server fault. The status now comes from the error itself, so all eight call
sites agree and later variants are classified where they are defined rather
than at each use. Scoped to the two cases those routes advertise; an unavailable
signing quorum is arguably transient too, but reclassifying it is not what this
change is for.

* test(credential-proxy): cover the status codes the ticketbook routes advertise

`status_code` shipped without a test. Pins the two retryable conditions to
503, and keeps `UninitialisedDkg` on the 500 side: nothing resolves it on
its own, so a caller retrying against it would loop forever.

* test(credential-proxy): cover the rotation gates behind a narrow epoch seam

Nothing taking `&ChainClient` could be exercised, since it wraps a real
signing client. The gates read exactly one chain query, so that is all
`EpochSource` exposes; the write path and the aggregation caches keep
taking the concrete client.

The trait stays `pub` and allows `async_fn_in_trait`: `pub(crate)` only
trades that warning for four `private_bounds` ones, and the methods
cannot be narrowed to match because nym-node-status-api calls them too.
No `Send` bound is needed either - every call site instantiates with the
concrete `ChainClient`, so the handlers still get a `Send` future.

bugfix: fix various bugs within nym-api making future re-DKG smoother [vol4] (#7096)

* feat(coconut-dkg): record which epoch's keys are in service

The epoch id counts ceremonies started, not key generations produced, so
`epoch_id - 1` names the wrong epoch the moment a ceremony fails: the id
moves on and leaves behind an epoch that concluded nothing and never
will. Everything that resolves an issuing epoch derives it that way
today, so a single failed ceremony would have signers issuing under an
epoch with no aggregate key.

`update` records the epoch coming into service where it already stamps
the conclusion, and a fresh ceremony leaves both fields alone - starting
one, or failing one, retires nothing.

`is_ceremony_concluded` moves onto the same footing. Sitting below the
current id is not enough: an abandoned epoch does too, and treating it
as concluded lets callers memoise its empty signer set with no expiry.

* feat(coconut-dkg): seed the epoch in service on migration

An epoch already in service concluded its own ceremony, so recording it
is reading a fact off the chain rather than guessing one. Any other state
is left unknown: which epoch is in service is exactly what was never
stored, and deriving it from the epoch id is the guess this field exists
to remove. Unknown refuses issuance until the next conclusion writes the
truth, which is the behaviour from before mid-ceremony issuance existed.

Seeding matters for the first rotation rather than the second: a fresh
ceremony carries the recorded epoch forward, so without the seed the next
reset would run with nothing in service and stop issuance for its
duration - the very case mid-ceremony issuance was built for.

Skipped once anything is recorded. Re-seeding a concluded epoch would put
the same value back while clearing the epoch it superseded along with it,
dropping the window a collection begun under that epoch still needs.

* fix(nym-api): resolve the issuable epoch from the keys in service

`current - 1` is only the epoch in service while every ceremony has
concluded. A failed one moves the id on without producing keys, so the
signer would have named an epoch with no aggregate key: some signers hold
a derived key for it and would sign, others refuse, and the client is left
with sub-threshold shares bound to an epoch that can never reach it.

The grace window had the same arithmetic, so after a failure it would have
honoured an epoch nobody was ever collecting under while refusing the one
they were - stranding exactly the deposits it exists to protect.

Both now come off a single epoch snapshot, which also removes a smaller
hazard: the three separate cache reads this used to make could straddle a
ceremony concluding and answer from either side of it.

`current_ceremony_concluded_at` goes with them; the snapshot carries it,
and `issuable_epochs` was its only caller.

The dummy channel keeps the keys in service explicitly rather than
deriving them, gains `fail_ceremony`, and delegates the concluded check to
`Epoch::is_ceremony_concluded` so it cannot drift from the real rule.

* fix(credential-proxy): issue under the epoch in service, not the id below

Same defect as the signer side, in the proxy's own copy of the
arithmetic. `current - 1` names an epoch with no keys once a ceremony has
failed, and the liveness check treated any epoch id above zero as proof
that something had concluded - so a first ceremony being retried would
have read as healthy while nothing was issuable at all.

Both now ask the epoch which generation is in service. The retry case
refuses as `CredentialsNotYetIssuable`, which is a 503: the condition
clears the moment a ceremony concludes, so a caller should come back.

* fix(bandwidth-fetcher): pin the epoch in service rather than the id below

The client's own copy of the same two derivations. It states the issuance
epoch on every request now, so getting this wrong is worse here than
elsewhere: the epoch it names is the epoch its shares are signed under,
and an epoch a failed ceremony abandoned has no key to unblind them with.

The wait loop had the matching flaw - a non-zero epoch id was taken as
proof that something had concluded, so a first ceremony being retried
would have let the client through to buy a book nobody could sign.

bugfix: fix various bugs within nym-api making future re-DKG smoother [vol5] (#7107)

* feat(coconut-dkg): let the admin force a reset from any state

A ceremony that keeps ending sub-threshold auto-resets straight into the
next attempt without ever passing through `InProgress` - and `InProgress`
is the only state `TriggerReset` accepts. So the one failure mode that
needs admin intervention is the one state the admin lever cannot reach:
a looping ceremony can never be stopped or redirected.

`TriggerForcedReset` is a separate message rather than a widening of
`TriggerReset`, deliberately. The state gate on the ordinary lever is a
safety interlock - a slip mid-ceremony errors instead of aborting a
running exchange - and widening it would make the same message mean
different things on either side of the migration. A distinct name also
keeps the chain log self-describing: an emergency intervention reads as
one in a post-mortem.

The forced reset is refused only before initialisation. Its successor is
always a non-resharing attempt, aborted resharings included, since their
registrants may hold nothing to reshare; and `keys_in_service` is carried
over, so aborting an exchange retires nothing and issuance continues
under the epoch in service throughout.

Also fixes `try_trigger_reset` misreporting its refusal as
`CantReshareDuringExchange`; the reset variant existed unused, and
nothing matches on either.

The variant is additive and no query or state shape changes, so laggard
signers are unaffected.

* fix(nym-api): decide the signing keys' epoch on the guard actually served

keys_for_epoch read which epoch the live slot held, dropped the lock, and
re-acquired it to serve the keys - so a rotation landing between the two
reads served a keypair for a different epoch than requested, and both
partial-signature paths would persist the wrong-key result for good. The
check now happens on the guard that is returned, and the archive answers
whenever the live slot does not match - which also finds keys that moved
to the archive between the reads instead of erroring on where they were.

* fix(ecash): treat an already-lapsed epoch deadline as no deadline when caching

The settled epoch keeps the deadline of its last self-extension, and since
the extension's removal nothing will ever move it. Once that timestamp
passes, min(state_end - now, ceiling) goes negative and the cached copy
expires in the past - permanently invalid, so every epoch read on every
signer, the proxy and node-status-api goes to the chain from that moment
until the next ceremony stores a fresh epoch. A deadline already behind us
now falls back to the staleness ceiling, in both copies of the cache.

* feat(coconut-dkg): say on the transaction when an advance is held for dealers

The zero-dealer hold succeeds looking exactly like a real advance, so a
ceremony stuck waiting for dealers - the reset's likeliest failure mode if
signers are not ready - could only be noticed by diffing successive epoch
queries. The held branch now emits awaiting_dealers with the held epoch's
id, making the condition visible on the transaction itself and alertable
from the event stream. A real advance stays attribute-free, pinned by test.

* docs(ecash): true up the comments the stack review flagged

Drop the stale 'Currently RED' markers (green since the fixes landed in
the same commits), state the guarantee is_ceremony_concluded actually
provides (nothing at-or-below the in-service epoch can change again; an
abandoned epoch below it reads concluded but is equally frozen), match
corrupt_vk_share's doc to the closure it takes, and move a doc comment
above its #[instrument] attribute.

* test(nym-api): make the dummy's ceremony start mirror the chain's

start_ceremony now clears ceremony_concluded_at and carries outgoing_keys
across, as next_ceremony does; previously the two divergences compensated
for each other through issuable_epochs, which a future test relying on
either mid-ceremony field would not survive. keys_in_service stays
synthesized from the id below: the helper doubles as a state constructor
paired with set_epoch, and its callers build their states through it.

* test(ecash): pin the reason in the review's flagged broad asserts

Three assertions accepted any failure where a specific one was the point:
the non-member registration now asserts the cw4 group-check refusal (and
derives its outsider address like every other, instead of hardcoding a
bech32), the stale-order replay asserts the exact StaleVerificationOrder
variant with both epoch ids, and the test dummy's verify arm now binds the
order's epoch_id and asserts it against the chain's, mirroring the gate
the real contract applies.
